name: Fes
tagline: The most complete medieval city in the Arab world, a car-free maze of madrasas, tanneries and workshops that has barely changed in centuries.
highlight: A guided walk through Fes el-Bali, ending on a terrace above the tanneries.
shortDescription: Morocco's spiritual and cultural capital: a 9th-century medina of thousands of lanes, the world's oldest surviving university, ornate madrasas and traditional crafts.
metaDescription: A Fes travel guide: Fes el-Bali medina, Al-Qarawiyyin, the tanneries, Bou Inania Madrasa, Bab Boujloud, riads, food, how to avoid getting lost and a three-day plan.
knownFor: The medina, tanneries, madrasas, craft workshops, Al-Qarawiyyin
goodFor: History, crafts, food, architecture, a medieval atmosphere

image.alt: The blue-tiled Bab Boujloud gate at the entrance to the medina of Fes

intro: Fes was founded in 789 by Idris I, and his son Idris II made it his capital around 809. It grew as a centre of learning and trade, receiving waves of refugees from Córdoba and Kairouan in the 9th century, and it has been the intellectual and religious capital of Morocco for much of the time since. UNESCO inscribed the medina in 1981.

The old city, Fes el-Bali, is one of the largest car-free urban areas in the world. Thousands of lanes wind between houses, workshops, fondouks (caravan inns), fountains and mosques, and mules and handcarts carry everything. It is easy to be overwhelmed, and even harder to get out, but with a guide for the first morning, it becomes a place of extraordinary craftwork and quiet corners.

Al-Qarawiyyin, founded in 859 by Fatima al-Fihri, is often described as the oldest continuously operating university in the world. Around it stand the great Marinid madrasas of the 14th century, and outside the walls the newer Ville Nouvelle offers cafés and more modern hotels.

whyVisit.intro: Fes is the best place in Morocco to feel the country's medieval past, and one of the great historic cities of the Islamic world.

points.title: A living medieval city
points.text: Craftspeople still make brass, leather, ceramics and textiles in the same quarters, by the same methods, as their predecessors.

points.title: Superb Islamic architecture
points.text: The Bou Inania and Al-Attarine madrasas are covered in carved cedar, stucco and zellige tile.

points.title: The tanneries
points.text: The Chouara tannery, with its stone vats of dye, is one of the most photographed and pungent sights in Morocco.

points.title: Real food
points.text: Fes is regarded as the culinary capital of the country, and its pastilla and rich stews are celebrated.

points.title: Fewer resorts, more life
points.text: Fes remains a working city, and the medina is a place where people live, shop and pray.

attractionsIntro: The main sights are in Fes el-Bali. Hire a guide for the first day and then explore alone.

attractions.name: Bab Boujloud
attractions.text: The blue-tiled gate, from 1913, at the western entrance to the medina. Blue outside, green inside, the colours of the city and of Islam.
attractions.tip: Enter here for the most gradual introduction to the medina.

attractions.name: The Chouara tannery

image.alt: The colourful stone vats of the Chouara tannery in Fes, seen from above

attractions.text: A medieval leather tannery where hides are soaked in vats of dye and pigeon droppings. Visitors watch from the terraces of leather shops, which give out sprigs of mint.
attractions.tip: Best in the morning, and you are expected to browse the shop.

attractions.name: Al-Qarawiyyin and its library

image.alt: The courtyard of the University of al-Qarawiyyin in Fes

attractions.text: The mosque and university founded in 859. The interior is closed to non-Muslims, but the gates and courtyard can be glimpsed from outside, and its restored library has reopened to visitors at times.
attractions.tip: Ask your guide about the library's current opening.

attractions.name: Bou Inania Madrasa
attractions.text: A 14th-century Marinid college with a courtyard of cedar, marble and tile, one of the few religious buildings in Morocco open to non-Muslims.
attractions.tip: Visit early for the best light.

attractions.name: Al-Attarine Madrasa
attractions.text: A smaller, more intimate 14th-century madrasa with immaculate decoration, next to the spice market.
attractions.tip: Combine it with the spice and perfume stalls.

attractions.name: Fes el-Jdid and the Mellah
attractions.text: The 13th-century royal quarter and the old Jewish quarter, with distinctive balconies, the palace gates and a Jewish cemetery.
attractions.tip: Go by petit taxi, since it is outside the medina.

attractions.name: The Borj Nord and the Marinid Tombs
attractions.text: Hilltop viewpoints above the medina, which give the classic panorama of the old city.

thingsToDoIntro: Fes rewards a slow rhythm, and wandering with a purpose, whether shopping, eating or learning a craft.

thingsToDo.title: Take a guided medina walk
thingsToDo.text: A licensed guide takes you through the main lanes, explains the crafts and keeps you from getting lost. Book through a riad for a fair price.
thingsToDo.tip: Agree the price and the length in advance.

thingsToDo.title: Watch the craftspeople
thingsToDo.text: The Seffarine Square coppersmiths, the weavers, the woodcarvers and the potters all work in the open.

thingsToDo.title: Take a cooking class
thingsToDo.text: Learn to make a tagine or pastilla in a riad kitchen, after a shopping trip to the market.

thingsToDo.title: Visit the pottery at Ain Nokbi
thingsToDo.text: The potteries outside the medina fire the celebrated blue Fassi ceramics, and offer demonstrations.
thingsToDo.tip: Combine with the Borj Nord view.

thingsToDo.title: Look at the city from above
thingsToDo.text: The Marinid Tombs on the hill give a sweeping view over the medina, and are quietest at dusk.

thingsToDo.title: Base yourself for day trips
thingsToDo.text: Meknes, Volubilis and Chefchaouen are all within reach. See [[meknes-volubilis|Meknes and Volubilis]].
thingsToDo.tip: Ask your riad to arrange a driver.

foodIntro: Fassi cuisine is considered the most refined in Morocco, based on rich sauces, pastry and slow cooking.

foods.name: Pastilla
foods.text: The famous pigeon or chicken pie in paper-thin pastry with almonds, cinnamon and sugar.

foods.name: Rfissa
foods.text: Shredded msemen pancakes with chicken, lentils and fenugreek in a spiced broth, traditionally served to new mothers.

foods.name: Bissara
foods.text: A thick, warming fava bean soup with olive oil and cumin, eaten for breakfast in winter.

foods.name: Fassi tagine
foods.text: Lamb or chicken cooked with dried fruit, saffron and preserved lemon.

foods.name: Msemen and harcha
foods.text: Flat breads and semolina cakes eaten for breakfast with honey and butter.

foods.name: Mint tea and pastries
foods.text: Sweet pastries and tea in a café or riad courtyard.

accommodation.intro: Staying in the medina is a major part of the Fes experience, and riads range from simple to palatial.

areas.name: Fes el-Bali
areas.text: Riads near Bab Boujloud and the Bou Inania are easiest to reach.

areas.name: Fes el-Jdid
areas.text: Guesthouses and small hotels near the Royal Palace.

areas.name: Ville Nouvelle
areas.text: The French-built new town, near the station.

gettingThere.intro: Fes is about 200 km east of Rabat and 300 km north-east of Marrakech.

options.text: About 4 hours from Casablanca and 3 hours from Rabat.
options.detail: First class is cheap and comfortable.

options.text: Direct flights from several European cities, and from Casablanca.
options.detail: The airport is 20 minutes from the centre.

options.text: CTM buses from Chefchaouen (about 4 hours) and Meknes (about 1 hour).

gettingAround.intro: Fes el-Bali has no cars, and the rest of the city is served by taxis.

options.text: The only way in the medina.
options.detail: Wear good shoes, and mind mules in the lanes.

options.text: Cheap taxis take you between the gates and the new town.
A licensed guide is the best way to find a route.

bestTime.headline: March–May and September–November
bestTime.summary: Fes is inland and has hot summers and cool, wet winters.

seasons.text: Cold and wet at times, but few visitors.

bestTime.avoid: July and August. The Festival of World Sacred Music in spring draws crowds.

itinerary.title: Two days in Fes
itinerary.intro: The classic medina sights with a guide on the first day and self-guided exploring on the second.

days.title: The medina with a guide
days.morning: Bab Boujloud, the Bou Inania Madrasa and the crafts quarters.

days.title: On your own
days.morning: Al-Attarine Madrasa and the spice market.
days.afternoon: Fes el-Jdid and the Mellah, or a cooking class.

tipsIntro: Fes is a maze, and a few tips make it easier.
tips: Hire a licensed guide for the first morning. They keep touts away and orient you.
Ignore anyone who says a street is closed or that a shop is not open.
Make a note of your riad's name and gate. Landmarks help.
Move out of the way of donkeys and mules when you hear 'balak'.
Take cash for shopping and taxis.
The tannery visit is best in the morning.
Fridays are quieter, with shops closed at midday for prayer.

faq.q: How many days do you need in Fes?
faq.a: Two or three. One day gives you a taste, but the medina rewards a slower pace.

faq.q: Do I need a guide in Fes?
faq.a: It is strongly recommended for the first morning. The medina has thousands of lanes, and a licensed guide helps you navigate and avoid unofficial ones.
Yes, for most visitors. Expect hassle from touts, and take care of valuables in crowded lanes.
Fes is older, more authentic and less polished. Marrakech is livelier and easier. Many visitors do both.

faq.q: Can non-Muslims enter mosques in Fes?
faq.a: Generally no. The Bou Inania Madrasa and some others are open as historic monuments, but most mosques are closed to non-Muslims.

faq.q: Is the tannery smell that bad?
faq.a: It is pungent, and shops give mint sprigs to hold to your nose. It is worth seeing.
